concepts.description: A unit of money used to express value, with an ISO 4217 code. Values are keyed by the lowercase alphabetic code. Starter subset: three currencies. No alias is a bare word or symbol that several currencies share ("dollar", "$"): the US dollar is "US dollar", "US dollars" or "US$", so another dollar can be added without a collision.

An amount of money. It is only meaningful together with its currency: its unit is one of the values of currency, so a concept that extends it states the currency as that value (unit: USD), and the check resolves the unit to exactly one currency. A dataset that does not store the currency must still say which one applies.

An indicative reference observation relating two currencies in an explicit direction, for a stated reference date and under a provider's methodology. It is not a transaction execution rate, tradable bid or ask, live tick, daily average or closing price. The same date and currency pair may be republished; those fields alone do not identify an immutable observation.

The calendar date to which a reference quote applies, without a time of day or time zone. It does not assert a publication, retrieval, transaction or rate-setting instant, or an observation at midnight.

The currency in the denominator of a directed reference quote. The rate expresses quote-currency units per one unit of this currency. A model may state it as explicit context when the source omits a base-currency field.

The currency in the numerator of a directed reference quote. Its code identifies a currency; it does not identify a country, territory, tender validity interval or a transaction currency. Missing quotes do not imply a zero rate or permission to substitute a successor currency.

The positive ratio of quote-currency units per one base-currency unit for an indicative reference quote. The pair direction, reference date and provider methodology are necessary context. It is not a money amount, reciprocal, cross-rate, execution price, bid or ask, daily average or closing price. Reversing the pair or combining quotes is a separate derivation requiring an explicit arithmetic and rounding policy; rates must not be summed as amounts.

document.description: Value and money expressed as reusable concepts: currencies and amounts of money.
document.name: Assets and finance

concepts.description: A calendar day: year, month and day, without a time of day. A dataset that stores a timestamp whose time is always midnight can treat it as a date. Questions that ask "when", "which year" or "which month" group by a date.

document.description: Time concepts that keep their meaning across representations.
document.name: Calendar and time

concepts.description: A person or organization that purchases goods or services.

A request for payment for goods or services supplied to a customer: what was supplied, when, where it is billed, and the amount charged. Not an order (a request to supply) and not a receipt (proof of payment). A dataset whose invoices are purchases says so with its own synonyms.
One item on an invoice, with its unit price and quantity.
A request or commitment to supply goods or services. An order describes intended supply; an invoice requests payment for supplied goods or services, and a receipt records payment.
One product or service entry on a commercial order or invoice, commonly with a quantity and a unit price. It does not by itself specify whether the document requests supply or payment.
One product or service requested on an order.
The amount charged on an invoice, normally the sum of its lines.
The amount asked for one unit of a product or service, such as the list price in a catalogue. The amount actually charged on a sale is a unit-price.
The price charged for one unit of an item on an invoice line.
How many units of an item were sold on one line.
The money received from sales over a period, before costs. From the buyer's side the same number is spend, so a question about who buys or spends the most asks for revenue grouped by the buyer.

measure.formula: The sum of the invoice totals of the sales in scope.

document.description: Buying and selling: customers, orders, invoices, line items, prices and revenue.
document.name: Commerce

concepts.description: A group coordinating people toward a shared purpose; membership does not require a separate legal organization.
The name used for the team.
An organization with which the team is associated.
A person participating in the team.
A route for contacting the team.
A subdivision of an organization with a defined operating responsibility.
The name of the subdivision.
The organization of which this is a subdivision.
The operating remit of the subdivision.
A route for contacting the subdivision.
A communication endpoint used to reach a person, organization or group; it is not the person or place itself.
The communication medium, such as email or telephone.
The address or identifier used on that channel.
The reason to use this communication endpoint.
A person reachable through this endpoint.
An organization reachable through this endpoint.
A location where something can be situated or occur; distinct from the address used to describe it.
The name used for the location.
An address describing the location.
The civil time zone used at the location.
A description distinguishing this location.
A structured description used to locate a place or direct deliveries; distinct from the physical place.
The thoroughfare and premises description.
The town or locality in the address.
The postal routing code, where applicable.
The country in which the address is located.
A named set of civil time rules, including changes in UTC offset; distinct from a fixed offset.
The identifier naming the time rules in a stated naming system.
The system defining the time-zone identifier, such as IANA tzdb.
A human-readable label for these time rules.
The geographic or operational use of the time zone.
A type or model of good offered for supply; distinct from an individual asset that realizes it.
The name of the product offering.
The model identifier assigned to this product.
The characteristics of this product offering.
An organization offering this product.
An activity or capability offered for another party, rather than a physical product unit.
The name of the offered service.
The activity or capability supplied.
An organization providing the service.
A person providing the service.
A transfer of money between parties; distinct from a request to pay or an outstanding obligation.
The monetary amount recorded for the transfer.
The recorded currency of the transfer amount.
The date on which the transfer is recorded.
An organization acting as payer.
A person acting as payer.
An account through which the payment is recorded.
A duty to pay an amount to another party; distinct from the payment that may discharge it.
The original monetary amount committed by the obligation, distinct from its outstanding balance.
The currency in which the obligation amount is recorded.
An invoice providing context for the obligation.
An organization owing the payment.
A person owing the payment.
The date by which payment is due.
An account recording monetary holdings or transactions for a party; not necessarily a bank account.
The name used to identify the account.
An account identifier in the relevant accounting system.
A currency in which account entries are recorded.
An organization holding the account.
A person holding the account.
An agreement creating commitments between parties; distinct from a document that records the agreement.
The name used for the agreement.
The identifier used to refer to the agreement.
An organization participating as a party.
A person participating as a party.
A document recording evidence of the agreement.
An individually tracked resource used or controlled by a party; distinct from its product model.
The identifier assigned to this individual resource.
The name used for this resource.
The product model realized by this asset.
An organization responsible for custody.
A person responsible for custody.
A location at which the asset is situated.
A dispatch of goods between locations; distinct from the order requesting the goods.
The identifier used to track this dispatch.
An order whose fulfilment involves the shipment.
An individually tracked resource carried by the shipment.
A destination of the shipment.
The recorded date of dispatch.
A coordinated undertaking aimed at a defined outcome, commonly realized through tasks.
The name used for the undertaking.
The outcome the undertaking aims to achieve.
A team participating in delivery.
An event that provides context for the undertaking.
A defined piece of work that can be assigned and tracked within an undertaking.
The name of the task.
A project containing this task.
A person assigned to perform the work.
An asset on which the work is performed.
A document used as evidence when performing or reviewing the work.
An observation informing the work.
An occurrence or planned gathering at a time and place; distinct from its reservation or organizing project.
The name of the occurrence.
The start date and time, interpreted with its stated time zone or offset.
The end date and time, interpreted with its stated time zone or offset.
The named civil time rules for event times.
A location at which the event occurs.
An organization coordinating the event.
An asset used in the event.
An arrangement setting aside a resource or place for a time interval; distinct from the event using it.
The identifier of the reservation.
A location set aside by the arrangement.
An event served by the arrangement.
The beginning of the reserved interval.
The end of the reserved interval.
The named civil time rules for reservation times.
An identifiable body of recorded information, which can provide evidence without being the agreement or activity itself.
The title of the recorded information.
The identifier used to retrieve the document.
The revision designation of this document record.
An asset described by the document.
The media type of the document representation.
A recorded finding about a subject at a time; it does not by itself establish failure, diagnosis or a safety limit.
The asset to which the finding refers.
The date and time at which the finding was observed.
The finding recorded about the subject.
The recorded value of the observed characteristic.
The unit used for the recorded value.
A person making the observation.
An agreement governing the requested supply.
An organization requesting the supply.
The order carrying this line.
The product requested on this line.
The service requested on this line.
The number of units requested on this order line.
An order providing context for this invoice.
The recorded currency of the invoice total.
A subdivision of the organization.
A team in which the person participates.
The unpaid amount remaining at the observation time of a balance snapshot.
The date and time at which the outstanding balance was recorded.
An obligation to which this payment relates; allocation amounts and many-to-many reconciliation belong in the consuming data model.

document.description: Reusable concepts connecting purchasing, events and asset maintenance.
document.name: Connected operations

concepts.description: A task tracked on a delivery backlog. An epic, a user story, a delivery task, a bug, a spike, and a technical-debt item are kinds of work item. The general task is any assignable piece of work, including work that is not on a delivery backlog. A technical step under a story is a delivery task, not a second meaning of task. A work item is not a support ticket. A requirement is a representation of a need. The work item is delivery work that may satisfy that need, and a user story's text often is that representation. When both are recorded, requirement work item links them.
Where this work item sits in the team's workflow. The state names belong to the team. Status is not priority, and it is not which sprint the item is in.

The order in which a delivery team intends to pick up this work item among the others. It is a planning decision. It is not bug severity, which grades a flaw, and it is not requirement priority, which grades a need. A bug is a work item, so it can carry a severity and this priority at the same time.

A relative estimate of size for a work item. The Scrum Guide does not define story points. Teams most often point a user story, and sometimes a bug or a spike. The points are not hours, and a total is not comparable across teams as a unit of time. An epic is usually left unpointed, because its size is the items under it. Velocity is the sum of points completed in one sprint. It is not this attribute on a single item.
A larger work item this one is split from, such as the epic of a user story. The parent is not the project and not the sprint.
A sprint this work item is taken into. An item can move to a later sprint; the sprint is not part of the item's identity. A team that does not use sprints leaves this empty.

A work item larger than one delivery increment, split into smaller work items such as user stories. The Scrum Guide does not define an epic. Some writers call an epic a large user story before it is split. In this graph the epic is the parent item, so it is not recorded as a user story. It is not a sprint. A sprint is a time box, and an epic can stay open across several of them. It is not a release. A release is a version made available for use, and it may contain work from several epics or from only part of one.

A work item for a small outcome valuable to a user, often told as who wants what and why. It is not the epic it was split from. A technical step under the story is a delivery task. It is not a use case. A use case narrates how an actor reaches a goal, with a main flow and alternatives, and is not itself a backlog item. The story's text is often a usable representation of a stakeholder need. In this graph the requirement is that representation when it is recorded on its own, and this story is the delivery item. Link them with requirement work item when both exist. The story is not an acceptance criterion. A criterion is a condition for accepting the story, a requirement, or a service.

A work item for a technical step that carries out part of a user story or another backlog item. Planning conversations often call this step a task. This graph already uses task for any assignable piece of work, and a user story and an epic are kinds of task, so this concept is the step under a story rather than another name for every task. It does not by itself promise an outcome a user receives, so it is not a user story. It is not a spike. A spike's result is knowledge, inside the spike's own time box.

A flaw in software, recorded as a work item so it can be corrected. Defect is another name for this same flaw. Testing glossaries treat bug, defect, and fault as that flaw in a work product. Some organizations also use defect for a flaw found after release and bug for one found before. That split records when it was found, so both words still name this concept. A bug is not an incident. The incident is an unplanned interruption of a running service, which a bug may cause. Many bugs are found before they harm anyone, and an incident can have a cause other than a bug. A bug is not technical debt. Debt can meet its specification and still make later change expensive. A failure is a loss of ability to operate to specification or to deliver the required outcome. The word error is not a synonym: ITIL uses it for a flaw or vulnerability that may cause incidents, software testing uses it for the human mistake that introduces a defect, and dependability writing uses it for a wrong internal state. A known error is a problem that has been analysed, not a name for this flaw.

How far the software's behavior departs from what was specified or expected, from data loss or a crash to a cosmetic miss. It grades the flaw. It does not say when a team will fix it; that order is the work item's priority. Incident severity grades impairment of a running service and is a different attribute. One flaw can have a bug severity and, once it hurts a service, an incident severity as well.
The sequence a person follows to make the flaw appear. It is evidence on the bug, not the severity and not the correction.

A work item that records a shortcut, a workaround left in place, or a design that has aged, where the cost appears as slower or riskier change later. The software may meet its requirements, so this is not a bug and not a defect. It is not an incident: nothing has to be failing now. It is scheduled with a priority, like any other work item.

A time-boxed work item whose result is knowledge: an answer that unblocks an estimate or a design. The practice comes from Extreme Programming and is used with Scrum. The Scrum Guide does not define it. It does not promise an outcome a user receives, so it is not a user story. It is not a bug. The time box belongs to the spike. A sprint is the team's iteration and is not another name for a spike.

A fixed-length iteration in which a team takes on a set of work items. In Scrum a sprint lasts at most one month. It has a start day and an end day. Work left unfinished stays a work item. It does not become a property of the sprint. A sprint may be run inside a project and may be recorded with none. The Scrum Guide does not make a sprint a part of a project, and it does not define story points or velocity. A sprint is not a release and not a deployment.
The project this sprint is part of, when the team runs it inside a project. A sprint can be recorded with no project.
The calendar day the sprint starts.
The calendar day the sprint ends.

A version made available for use. For software, release version names that version. A release of a service, with no software version, leaves the version empty. The same release can be deployed more than once and into more than one environment. A release is not a deployment, not a build, and not an environment. It is not a sprint. A feature flag can change what users see of a release that is already deployed, without making another release.
The software version this release makes available. The version identifies the software; the release is the decision to offer it.
A work item included in this release. The work item is not the release, and a deployment of the release is a further fact.

The act of putting a build into an environment. The same release can be deployed many times, and a deployment can fail to reach the environment while the release still exists. A deployment is not a release, not a version, and not the environment it targets. It is not a change request. The change request is the proposal, and a deployment is one way that proposal is carried out. Putting bytes into an environment is not the same as showing new behavior to users. A feature flag can do that with no further deployment. Whether the deployment reached the environment, and whether it then required remediation, is the deployment outcome.
The environment the build is put into. A deployment to staging and a deployment to production are different deployments even when they carry the same release.
When the deployment was carried out. The record may be a calendar day or an instant. It is not the identity of the release and not the version number.
The release this deployment puts into an environment, when the deployment is of a named release. Deploying a build that was never named as a release leaves this empty.
The build that was put into the environment.

What this deployment did: whether it reached the target environment, and whether the service then had to be remediated, for example by a rollback or a follow-up fix. A deployment that never reaches production is not counted in deployment frequency and is not a change failure. A deployment that reaches production and degrades the service is counted in the frequency and in the change failure rate. The outcome of one deployment is not either of those rates.
The change request this deployment carries out, when one is recorded. A deployment can have no change request, and a change can be carried out by something other than a deployment.

A proposal to bring one or more commits into a line of development. A merge request is that same proposal under another tool's name. The proposal is not a code review: the review is an examination of it, and one proposal can have several reviews. It is not a change request, which judges a change to a service, and it is not a deployment.
The repository whose line of development the proposal targets.
An examination of a pull request by a person, recorded as remarks or a decision. The review is not the pull request. Several reviews can belong to one pull request.
The pull request this review examines.

The sum of story points on the work items a team completed in one sprint. The Scrum Guide does not define velocity. It is a planning aid for that team. It is not a count of hours, not deployment frequency, and not a unit that can be compared across teams as time. Adding the velocities of several sprints does not produce a larger velocity. The reading belongs to one sprint. Velocity is not a DORA delivery metric.

measure.formula: The sum of the story points of the work items completed in the sprint.

concepts.description: The elapsed time from when work starts on a work item until that work is finished. It is not lead time for changes, which runs from a commit until the change is running in production. It is not the wait from a request arriving until delivery; that longer interval is sometimes also called lead time, and it is not this measure. The length of a sprint is not a cycle time.

measure.formula: For a finished work item, the elapsed time from the start of work until the work is finished. A figure for a team over a window is recomputed from the items in that window.

concepts.description: How often changes are successfully deployed to production, as a count per unit of time over a stated window. This is one of DORA's software delivery metrics, with lead time for changes, change failure rate, and failed deployment recovery time. A deployment that does not reach production is not counted. A deployment that reaches production and later needs remediation is still counted. The share that needs remediation is the change failure rate. One named release can be deployed more than once, so this counts deployments. A release to end users with no separate deployment, such as turning a feature flag on, counts when the team treats that release as the production release, and is not counted again when it is the same event as a deployment.

measure.formula: The number of deployments that reached production in the window, divided by the length of the window. A deployment that never reaches production is excluded. Recomputed for the window.

concepts.description: How long a change takes from a commit until it is deployed in production. This is one of DORA's software delivery metrics. The clock ends at the production deployment, not when a feature flag later exposes the change and not when a customer first asked for it. Over a window, this measure is the median of those durations, which is how the Four Keys measurement summarizes them. DORA's survey asks for the typical time. A mean of the same durations is a different summary and is not this measure. The interval is not cycle time, which starts when work starts rather than at the commit, and it is not the time from a customer request until delivery. Both of those are sometimes called lead time. This concept is only commit to production deployment. It is not deployment frequency.

measure.formula: The median, over changes deployed to production in the window, of the elapsed time from the commit until that production deployment.

concepts.description: The proportion of production deployments, including releases to users that the team counts as deployments, that degrade the service and need remediation such as a hotfix, a rollback, or a fix forward. A bug found before production is outside the rate. So is an incident that a deployment did not cause, and a pipeline run that never reached production. DORA's later deployment rework rate, the proportion of deployments that are unplanned work to fix defects, is not this rate. This is one of DORA's software delivery metrics. It is not deployment frequency, which is a count of deployments that reached production, per unit of time.

measure.formula: The number of production deployments in the window that degrade the service and require remediation, divided by the number of production deployments in that window. A deployment that never reaches production is in neither count. Recomputed for the window.

document.description: How software work moves from a backlog to a running environment: work items, iterations, releases, deployments and the measures of that flow.
document.name: Software delivery

concepts.description: A country or territory with an ISO 3166-1 code, identified independently of any data source. Values are keyed by the lowercase ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code. A dataset that stores a country by name matches it against a value's labels and aliases; one that stores a code matches it against the value's codes.

en: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

concepts.description: An ISO 3166-1 code that identifies a country: alpha-2 ("IE"), alpha-3 ("IRL") or numeric ("372"). Each country value lists all three.
A named settlement located within a country. No known values yet: city names repeat across countries, so a dataset matches a city together with its country.
The number of people living in a country at a point in time. Always state the year: populations change every year and sources differ.

measure.formula: The count of residents of the country in the stated year.

document.description: Places with a meaning shared across datasets: countries, cities, and the people who live in them. Starter subset: the country list holds a starter set of countries; the full ISO 3166-1 list comes later.
document.name: Geography

concepts.description: An individual human being.
A group with a defined identity and purpose, such as a company.
A person employed by an organization.
The employee that another employee reports to.

document.description: People, organizations, and the roles people hold in an organization.
document.name: People and organizations

concepts.description: The depth of a support response. Level 1 takes the report, applies a known fix or a runbook, and passes on what it cannot close. Level 2 investigates further, often the people who operate the application. Level 3 is specialist depth: a change to the software, a vendor, or the team that builds it. Organizations draw those boundaries differently, and some add another tier, so the three levels are the usual case rather than a closed list. A tier is not an on-call rotation, which says who is reachable now, and not a priority, which says how soon a ticket should be worked.
The name this organization uses for the tier, such as Level 1, L2, or a vendor's own name. The name is not a priority.

A tracked request for attention from the people who operate a service. An incident and a service request are kinds of support ticket. A problem is not one: it follows a cause across incidents rather than one report. A ticket is not a work item on a delivery backlog, though repairing the cause may add one.
A person currently responsible for the ticket.
A team currently responsible for the ticket.
The support tier currently responsible for the ticket. An escalation moves the ticket from one tier to another. The tier is not the ticket's priority.

An unplanned interruption to a service, or a reduction in its quality. The incident is that interruption. Restoring the service is why it is handled, and can finish before the cause is understood. A problem is the cause, or a potential cause, and can sit behind several incidents. A service request asks for a service action already agreed as normal delivery; nothing has to have failed. A bug is a flaw recorded as delivery work and may never reach a running service. An incident can also come from configuration, capacity, or a dependency, with no bug. A change request proposes a modification. An emergency change may be what restores the service; the request is still not the incident.

How badly the service is impaired, on the scale the organization uses for operations. A low number is not universally the worst grade. Severity is not impact, which is the business effect, and not urgency, which is how soon restoration is needed. It is not priority. Priority is the order of work and can diverge from the grade: a severe fault in a service with no users until morning is not the same queue position as a moderate fault that blocks today's payroll. ITIL names impact, urgency, and priority for this ordering, and does not define severity as that order.

The effect of this incident on users or on a business process, such as which work is blocked. Impact is not urgency and not priority. It is not severity, the operations grade of the impairment. Teams often align the grade and the effect, and the two can still differ.

How quickly the business needs the service restored. Urgency is not impact. A severe impairment of a service that nobody needs until morning can have low urgency. Practices often suggest a priority from impact and urgency. Incident priority stores the order that was chosen, including when a person overrides that suggestion.

The order in which responders work this incident. It is often chosen from impact and urgency, and a person can override that suggestion. The attribute stores the resulting order, not the impact and not the urgency. It is not severity, which grades the impairment, and it is not the support tier that holds the ticket.

Where this incident sits between being recorded and being closed. Practices often distinguish open, restored and resolved, but the names belong to the practice. Status is not severity. Resolved, on the record, can differ from restored, on the service.
The service whose quality is interrupted or reduced. A failing software component may be what broke the service; the service is still what the users were promised.

The instant the incident was recorded. The service may have failed earlier; that instant is the incident failure time when it is known. This instant is not when the service was restored and not when a person acknowledged an alert.
The instant the incident record was marked resolved, often because a workaround or a fix is in place. That can be earlier or later than the instant the service was restored.
The instant the service met its success criterion again. Mean time to restore ends at this instant, not at the resolved time of the record and not at the time an alert was acknowledged.

The instant the service was interrupted or its quality dropped, when that instant is known. The record may have been opened later. Mean time to restore is measured from this instant, not from the opened time and not from acknowledgement of an alert.

A way to reduce or avoid the impact of this incident without removing the cause. It may restore the service for now. It can be found before any problem has been analysed. It is not the root cause and not a permanent removal of the cause.

A bug recorded as a cause of this incident, when the harm comes from a software flaw. The attribute is absent when the cause is something else. Linking the two does not make the incident a bug or the bug an incident.

A request from a user, or from that user's authorized representative, that starts a service action already agreed as a normal part of delivery, such as granting access or supplying information. Nothing has to have failed, so a service request is not an incident. It is not a change request. A standard change, pre-authorized for that kind of request, may be how the request is fulfilled. The request and the change stay different records.

A cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents. The work is to understand that cause and to make a repeat less likely or less harmful. Restoring the service belongs to the incident and can finish while the problem stays open. A problem is not a change request. A change is one way the cause might be removed, and the request for that change is a separate record. When the problem has been analysed and is not yet resolved, it is a known error. A documented workaround is not what makes it one. A workaround can be recorded earlier.

The cause the investigation has settled on, when it has one. A known error means the problem has been analysed and is not yet resolved; the root cause can still be only partly identified. The cause is not the workaround that reduces the effect.
An incident this problem is taken to explain. One problem can sit behind several incidents. The incident remains the record of restoring the service.

A problem that has been analysed and has not been resolved. Analysis is what distinguishes it from a problem that is still unexamined. A workaround is often recorded with it and is not required for this status. The cause can still be in the service, so a known error is not a completed fix, not an incident, and not a runbook. It is not the ITIL word error, which names a flaw or vulnerability that may cause incidents. A runbook may tell a responder to apply a workaround.

A way to reduce or eliminate the impact of this problem when a full resolution is not yet available. It can be recorded before the problem has been analysed far enough to be a known error. It is not the root cause. A runbook may quote it. The workaround is not the runbook. An incident can carry a workaround of its own before a problem is opened.

A request for change: the recorded proposal to add, modify, or remove something that could affect a service, used so the risk can be judged before the change is made. The change itself is that addition, modification, or removal. This record is the proposal, not the incident it may help restore and not the problem whose cause it may remove. An emergency change is often how a service is restored; the request is still not the incident. It is not a release and not a deployment. A release is a version made available for use. A deployment puts a build into an environment, which is one way a change is carried out. A standard change may fulfill a service request. The request and the change stay different records.

How this change is authorized. A standard change is low-risk, pre-authorized, and fully documented, so it needs no further authorization. A normal change is assessed and authorized before it goes ahead. An emergency change must be introduced as soon as possible, often to restore a service. The words belong to the practice. The type is not the risk grade and not the deployment that carries the change out.
The assessed chance that this change harms the service, and how bad that harm would be, used to choose how the change is approved. It is not incident severity and not bug severity.
A problem this change is intended to remove or reduce. The change request remains a proposal; accepting it is not the same as closing the problem.

Sharing awareness of a support ticket, or transferring its ownership: to a deeper support tier, to another team, or to a manager. It happens at a time. It is not an event in this graph. An event here is an occurrence or a gathering at a time and place. An escalation is not a change of priority and not a change request. Moving from level 1 to level 2 is an escalation, and so is moving to level 3. The tiers are support tiers, not priorities.
The support ticket being handed on.
The support tier that hands the ticket on, when the escalation is from one tier to another.
The support tier that receives the ticket. A notice to a manager may name a person instead of a tier; that person is not a support tier.

The schedule of people responsible for answering alerts outside ordinary staffing. Any support tier can be on call, so the rotation is not a tier. It is not an alert and not an incident: it says who responds, not what failed.
The team whose members take turns on the rotation.
A person who takes a turn on the rotation. Not every member of the team is on the rotation.

An observation that a stated condition was met and that a person may need to act. It does not by itself establish the cause, the severity, or that an incident has occurred: several alerts can be one incident, and an alert can be a false signal. An alert is not a log entry. A log entry is a line the software wrote; an alert may be raised because of log entries.
The service whose condition the alert is about.
The instant a person accepts responsibility for the alert. Mean time to acknowledge ends at this instant and starts when the alert is raised. Acknowledgement is not restoration of the service.
The instant the alert was raised. Mean time to acknowledge runs from this instant until a person acknowledges the alert. Raising the alert is not restoration of the service.

A document of steps for operating a service or for handling a known situation, written so a responder can follow it under pressure. It is not a postmortem, which records an incident after the fact, and not a known error, which records a cause and a workaround. The runbook may tell the reader to apply a workaround.
The service whose operation this runbook describes.

A document written after an incident, once the service is restored, recording what happened, how the service was restored, what contributed, and what will change. It is not the incident record, not the problem record, and not a runbook. A meeting about how a sprint went is a different practice and is not this document.
The incident this document reviews. Writing the document does not reopen or replace the incident.

A documented agreement between a service provider and a customer that identifies the services required and the expected level of service. It creates commitments between those parties, which is why it is a contract in this graph. It is not the target figure and not the measurement. Those are the service level objective and the service level indicator. The SRE book tells an agreement apart from an objective by the consequence of a miss, such as a service credit: a target with no consequence is an objective, even if someone calls it an agreement. An agreement between internal teams, with no customer, is not this concept. A target with no documented agreement is an objective.
A service whose targets this agreement commits to.
An organization the agreement is with. This party defines the expected level with the provider. It need not be a purchasing customer.
A person the agreement is with, when the customer is a person rather than an organization.

A target value, or a range of values, for a service level over a stated window, measured by a service level indicator. One shape is a lower bound on a success proportion, such as 99.9 percent of valid requests. Another is a bound on a duration. It is not the agreement that may promise the target, and not the measurement that shows whether the target was hit. An objective can exist with no service level agreement. If nothing has been agreed to happen when the target is missed, the target is an objective. ITIL's service level is a metric of expected or achieved quality and does not split the target from the measurement; this concept is only the target. The unreliability a success-proportion target still allows is the error budget.

The target value over the objective's window, in the units of its indicator. A success proportion is a fraction of one: 99.9 percent is 0.999, not 99.9. A duration target is a duration. It is not the measured value. The service level indicator defines that measurement.
The service level indicator this objective sets a target against. The indicator is the measurement; the objective is the target.
A service level agreement that commits to this objective, when a customer is promised it. An internal objective can leave this empty.

A quantitative measure of one aspect of the level of service provided, such as the proportion of well-formed requests that succeed, a latency, or the proportion of time the service is usable. Each indicator names its own good events and valid events. Because that definition changes from one indicator to another, the indicator is an entity here and not one measure with a single formula. An objective sets a target on an indicator. The indicator is not that target and not the agreement. Availability is one measure a team may adopt as an indicator. A key performance indicator judges success against a business objective and is a different concept. ITIL's service level names expected or achieved quality without this split; this concept is only the measurement.
The service whose behavior this indicator measures.

The proportion of good events among valid events in a stated window, for the availability indicator the service uses. ITIL uses availability for the ability of a service to perform its agreed function when required. This concept is a measurement of that ability, not the ability itself and not a target. The SRE book defines it as the fraction of time a service is usable, and often implements that fraction as the yield of well-formed requests. Those two proportions answer different questions and must not be mixed in one figure. A duration of uptime is not this proportion. The proportion is not a service level objective and not a service level agreement.

measure.formula: Good events divided by valid events in the window. The service level indicator states which events count. Counting time, good events are the time the service could perform its agreed function. Counting requests, good events are the successful well-formed requests and valid events are the well-formed requests. One figure uses one of those definitions. Recomputed for the window.

concepts.description: The unreliability a success-proportion service level objective allows in its window: one minus the target. A 99.9 percent objective allows 0.1 percent. Applied to the valid events in the window, that proportion is a count of allowed bad events, which is the same allowance in the indicator's units. This measure is the allowance, not the amount still unused after failures have consumed some of it. It applies when the objective is a success proportion, the form the SRE workbook uses for an error budget. A target that is not a proportion, such as an average latency under a stated duration, is not turned into a budget by subtracting it from one. The budget is not a second objective and not availability.

measure.formula: One minus the objective's success-proportion target, with that target as a fraction of one. The count of bad events allowed in the window is that proportion times the valid events in the window. Recomputed for the window.

concepts.description: The proportion of the targets in one service level agreement that were met in a stated window. This proportion is defined here so several targets can be counted together. It is not a term from ITIL or from the SRE book, not availability, and not an error budget. It does not say which missed target carries a consequence. Meeting each target is decided on that target's own indicator.

measure.formula: The number of agreed service level targets met in the window, divided by the number of agreed targets that applied in the window. Recomputed for the window.

concepts.description: The arithmetic mean, over failures in a stated window, of the time from each failure until the service is restored. The failure instant is incident failure at when it is known, and restored is incident restored at: the service meets its success criterion again. That can differ from the time the incident record is marked resolved and from the time a person acknowledges an alert. ITIL calls this metric mean time to restore service (MTRS). The abbreviation MTTR is also used for mean time to repair, mean time to resolve, and mean time to recover, so it is not a synonym here. DORA's recovery metric is failed deployment recovery time. That metric covers only recovery from a failed deployment and is summarized as a median, not as this mean.

measure.formula: The sum of the restore durations of the failures in the window, divided by the number of those failures. Each duration runs from the failure instant until the service is restored.

concepts.description: The arithmetic mean, over alerts in a stated window, of the time from when an alert is raised until a person acknowledges it. Acknowledgement means someone accepts the alert. It is not restoration and not resolution of an incident. This mean is not mean time to restore, and it is not one of DORA's software delivery metrics.

measure.formula: The sum of the times from each alert in the window, starting when it is raised, until a person acknowledges it, divided by the number of those alerts.

concepts.description: How long it takes to restore service after a deployment, or a release to users, degrades the service and needs intervention. This is DORA's recovery metric, alongside deployment frequency, lead time for changes, and change failure rate. Until 2023 DORA asked for time to restore service after any user-impacting incident, which mixed failures caused by a change with failures from elsewhere, and that older question is not a synonym of this metric. A measured window is summarized by the median of the recovery durations. DORA's survey asks for the typical time rather than publishing a mean. The arithmetic mean of restore times for failures in general is mean time to restore. The clock ends when the service is restored, not when an alert is acknowledged and not merely when the incident record is closed.

measure.formula: The median, over failed deployments in the window, of the elapsed time from the deployment that caused the degradation until the service is restored. A failure that a deployment did not cause is excluded.

document.description: Running a service after it is built: support tickets, incidents, problems, changes, service levels and the response around them.
document.name: IT operations

concepts.description: A person, a group, or an organization with an interest in a change, a need, or a solution. BABOK includes groups. A group that is a team is recorded as the stakeholder's team, and an organization as the stakeholder's organization. A stakeholder is not a kind of person, because the interested party may be a team or an organization. The user named in a user story may be a stakeholder and may not be the only one. An employee may be a stakeholder and need not be.
The person who is this stakeholder, when the interested party is a person.
The organization that is this stakeholder, when the interested party is an organization.
The team that is this stakeholder, when the interested party is a group rather than one person or a whole organization.

A usable representation of a need. The classes are a business requirement, which states why a change has been initiated, a stakeholder requirement, which states what a stakeholder needs so that can be achieved, a solution requirement, which states a capability or quality of the solution as a functional or non-functional requirement, and a transition requirement, which is needed only while moving to the new state. A user story is a delivery work item whose text often represents a stakeholder need. The story and this requirement are linked when both are recorded, and they are not the same record. A use case narrates an interaction and is not one of these classes. An acceptance criterion is a condition for accepting a story, a requirement, or a service. Work that delivers the requirement is a work item, linked from the requirement.

How important this requirement is relative to others. One scheme is MoSCoW, which sorts requirements into must, should, could and won't. That is a priority classification. It does not grade the severity of a running failure or of a defect. A rank or another local scheme uses this same attribute. The scheme is not fixed here, and priority is not status.
A stakeholder who raised or owns this requirement. The source is not the user in every user story written from it.
Where this requirement sits between being proposed and being satisfied or dropped. The state names belong to the practice. Status is not priority.

A work item that delivers or checks this requirement. The link connects the recorded need to the delivery work. The work item does not replace the requirement, and a requirement can be met by more than one work item.
A business rule this requirement is meant to uphold. The rule can outlive the requirement, and the requirement is not the rule.

A requirement that states the goals, objectives, and outcomes for why a change has been initiated. It can apply to the whole organization, a business area, or one initiative. It is not a stakeholder requirement, which states what a stakeholder needs so those outcomes can be achieved, and it is not a functional requirement. It is not a user story. A story may represent part of the need and remains a work item.

A requirement that states what a stakeholder needs so the business requirements can be achieved. It bridges business requirements and solution requirements. It is not a business requirement and not a solution requirement. A user story often represents one of these needs and remains a work item, linked from the requirement when both are recorded.

A requirement that states a capability or a quality the solution must have to meet the stakeholder requirements, in enough detail to build and implement the solution. A functional requirement and a non-functional requirement are kinds of solution requirement. It is not a business requirement and not a transition requirement.

A solution requirement that states a capability the solution must have: the behavior and information the solution will manage. It is not a non-functional requirement, which states a condition or a quality such as speed, security, or availability. It is not a business rule. A rule constrains a decision whether or not this solution is built. It is not a use case. A use case narrates the steps of an interaction that may satisfy several functions.

A solution requirement that states a condition or quality of the solution rather than a function a user invokes: how fast it is, how it resists misuse, how available it is, how usable it is. BABOK also calls these quality of service requirements. Availability stated as a need is this kind of requirement. The measured availability of a running service is a different concept, and so is a service level objective, which is a target on a measurement. An objective may be how a quality requirement is checked in production. The objective is not the requirement.

A requirement that states a capability or condition needed only to move from the current state to the future state, such as converting data, training people, or keeping work going during the move. It is not needed once the change is complete. It is not a functional requirement of the future solution.

A description of how an actor reaches a goal by interacting with a system, including the main sequence and the alternatives. The actor may be a person, an organization, or another system. A use case is not a user story. The story is one backlog increment, while the use case is the interaction and can span more than one increment. It is not one of the requirement classes, though it may be written to show how requirements are met. It is not a business process. A business process is how the organization does a piece of work, whether or not that work is one session with a system.

The name of an actor in the use case. The actor may be a person, an organization, or another system, so this attribute is the name in the narrative rather than a reference to one kind of party. An actor need not be a stakeholder, because another system can be an actor, and need not be the only stakeholder of the requirements the use case touches.
A requirement this use case shows being met. The use case can touch several requirements, and a requirement can be met without a use case being written.

A condition that must be met before a user story, a requirement, or a service is accepted. ITIL states acceptance criteria for a service or a service component. Business analysis uses them for the minimum a solution must meet to be acceptable to key stakeholders, and delivery teams attach them to a user story. It is not the story text, not the requirement, and not a flow inside a use case. It is not an evaluation criterion, which ranks alternative solutions. One story or requirement can have several criteria. The plural acceptance criteria is the same concept.
The user story this condition is a check for, when it is attached to a story.
A requirement this condition is a check for, when it is attached to a requirement rather than only to a story.
A service this condition must be met for, when the criterion is stated for the service rather than for one story.

A specific, practicable, testable directive under the control of the business, which guides behavior or a decision. An example is a limit above which a second person must approve. It holds whether or not a particular solution is built. It is not a requirement. A requirement is a usable representation of a need a solution is expected to meet, though a requirement may exist so that a solution upholds a rule. It is not an acceptance criterion, which checks a story, a requirement, or a service.

A repeatable way the organization carries out a piece of its work: a sequence of steps with a reason to start and a result. It is not a use case, which is one actor's interaction with a system, and not a project, which is a temporary undertaking. Software can support a process; the process is not a software component.
One part of a business process: a single action or decision in that sequence. The step is not the whole process and not a work item on a delivery backlog.
The business process this step is part of.

A word with a stated meaning for a business domain, so that requirements, rules and processes use it in that meaning. It is not a requirement and not a business rule. The term defines a word; a rule constrains a decision.

A metric an organization has chosen to judge success in meeting an objective. Which formula it uses is part of that choice, so a key performance indicator is recorded as an entity and not as one measure with a formula fixed here. It is not a service level indicator. A service level indicator measures the behavior of a service. A key performance indicator judges a business result. An organization can watch either, and choosing one does not make it the other.
A business process whose performance this indicator is used to judge, when the indicator is about a process.

concepts.description: Software that people run. It may be offered outside the organization or used only inside the organization that builds it. It is not a product in this graph. A product is a type of good offered for supply. It is not a software component, which is a part of an application, and it is not one version, build, release, or deployment of the application. It is not the service users are promised. The service is the capability. An application may be what provides it.

A part of a software application, such as a module, a library or a microservice that is deployed on its own. Calling a part a microservice does not make it the service concept: a service is a capability offered to another party, and a component is a piece of software. A failing component may cause an incident on a service. The component is still not that service, and it is not the application taken as a whole.
An application this component is a part of.
A team accountable for this component.

An identified revision of a software application. A release uses a version as the name of what it makes available. A version is not a build. A build is one artifact produced from a commit, and building the same sources again can produce another artifact of the same version. A version is not a deployment and not an environment. The version number may follow semantic versioning or another scheme; the scheme is not part of the identity of this concept.
The identifier people use for this version, in whatever scheme the application uses. The number is not the release and not the build.
The application this version is a revision of.

A subset of infrastructure used for a particular purpose, where a build runs. The usual kinds are development, test, staging, and production. Development is where the software is changed. Test is where it is checked. Staging is a production-like place used to rehearse a release. Production is where the service's users are. Organizations use other names and other counts, so those four kinds are not a closed list. An environment is not a deployment into it and not a release. Software that runs in development is not, by that fact, running in production. The word can also mean external conditions. This concept is the infrastructure used for a purpose.

Which kind of place this environment is, in the organization's own words. Development, test, staging and production are the usual kinds. The attribute does not fix the vocabulary: a further kind, such as a sandbox, is still an environment type.

An artifact produced by building a commit: the bytes a deployment can put into an environment. A build is not a software version, though a team may store one identifier that is used for both, and it is not a release or a deployment. Two builds can exist for one version when the same sources are built again.
The commit this artifact was built from.
The software version this build is an artifact of, when the build is identified with a version. A build of a commit that has not been given a version leaves this empty.

A switch in running software that changes behavior without another deployment and without another release. The flag is usually shipped in a deployment while it is off. Turning it on is a separate act and is not itself a deployment. The same deployed build can behave differently for different users, or in different environments. A flag is not a version, not a build, and not an environment.
The application whose running behavior this flag changes.
An environment in which this flag is set, when the flag is not the same in every environment. The environment is where the software runs; the flag is not that place.

An interface through which one piece of software offers operations to another. The API is the interface as a whole. One operation of it is an API endpoint. An API is not a service, though a service may be reached through one, and it is not a deployment of the software that offers it.
The software component that offers this interface.
One operation of an API. Where the API uses HTTP, the operation has a method and a path. The endpoint is not the API as a whole and not a deployment.
The API this operation belongs to.
The method of the call. For an HTTP API this is the HTTP method, such as GET or POST. The method is not the path, and not every API uses HTTP methods.
The path of the operation, where the API identifies operations by a path. The path is not the method.
A store of the source of software, holding the commits of that source. It is not a build, not a release and not a document, though the source it holds may include documents.
An application whose source this repository stores. One application can have more than one repository.

A recorded revision of source in a repository. Lead time for changes is measured from a commit. A commit is not a build: the build is an artifact produced from a commit. It is not a pull request, which proposes one or more commits, and it is not a release.
The repository that holds this commit.

One line written by running software into its log. It is not an alert. An alert says a condition needs attention and may be raised because of log entries; the line is not that alert. It is not an incident.

How the software classified this line, in the scheme that software uses. Common grades run from a trace or debug line, through information and a warning, to an error. The names and the number of grades are not a closed list. A log level is not incident severity and not bug severity: it classifies a line the software wrote, not the impairment of a service and not a flaw on the backlog.
The instant the line was written. It is not the instant an incident was opened and not the instant an alert was acknowledged.
The software component that wrote the line.

An identity an application accepts when someone signs in. It is not a person: one person can hold several accounts, and an account can be recorded before it is tied to a person. It is not an employee. It is not a financial account.
The person this account is tied to, when that person is known. The account can exist without this link.
The application that accepts this account.

concepts.description: A pattern, not a number on its own: any measure for a place divided by the population of the same place, so that large and small places can be compared. It is a ratio, so it is never summed across places. A concept that extends it names the measure, the scale and the population source and year, and states its unit as the measure's unit per the scale's number of people (USD per million people).

measure.formula: The measure for a place, divided by the population of that place (same year where possible), multiplied by the scale (1 for "per person", 1,000,000 for "per million people").
